title: Rethinking Opinion Measurement Interfaces for Human-in-the-Loop Optimization

paper.title: Rethinking Opinion Measurement Interfaces for Human-in-the-Loop Optimization Note: First author’s note (2026): This paper was written in 2022 and is published here as last revised. Its central claim, that measuring human preferences is an interface design problem before it is a modeling problem, now matters far beyond human-in-the-loop optimization, including reinforcement learning from human feedback.
paper.abstract: Abstract. Human-in-the-loop optimization refers to systems that present choices to a human decision-maker and query their judgment to optimize system parameters iteratively. The user interface typically provides either an absolute rating scale or asks for a preferred option. However, these approaches can potentially suffer from calibration problems, inconsistencies, and completeness violations of user preferences in such a sequential evaluation. This paper revisits the design space of opinion measurement interfaces for human-in-the-loop optimization. We conducted a study (N=360) using text summarization and image color enhancement tasks to evaluate human sequential feedback in six representative opinion measurement interfaces. Based on our analysis, we recommend using a listwise approach to support sequential opinion measurement, which counterweighs individual rating and preferential choice limitations and conveys more information for subsequent use. We further discuss the trade-offs in different user interface designs and provide guidelines to inform future research.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text: Human-in-the-loop ( Monarch, 2021 ) (HITL) optimization has received increasing attention in HCI ( Zhou et al., 2021 ; Chan et al., 2022 ) . Such systems query decision makers for their judgment among machine proposals, e.g., using Bayesian optimization (BO) ( Kushner, 1964 ; Shahriari et al., 2016 ) as the background AI and then optimize underlying system parameters toward user preferences according to the feedback. One of the benefits is that this adaptation can support users to explore a design space ( Koyama et al., 2020 ; Yue et al., 2021 ; Chan et al., 2022 ) defined by finite criteria or retain more control over pre-configured system decision strategies ( Russell, 2019 ) . However, the opinion measurement interface ( Nobarany et al., 2012 ) used as input component in HITL optimization has many design parameters itself. Depending on the types of human feedback required, the whole process has different limitations due to the design of the input interface. For example, a commonly used pointwise user interface (UI) asks the user to rate a given option as utility-based direct feedback , see Figure 2 a. Although, literature has shown that humans are not good at absolute judgments ( Tversky and Kahneman, 1974 ) and tend to give local judgments ( Brochu et al., 2007a ) . Therefore, a rating interface could suffer from miscalibration and noisy human feedback, thus reducing human-AI cooperation performance. Another popular pairwise design ( Brochu et al., 2007a ; Christiano et al., 2017 ) is to ask humans which of the two given system outcomes is preferred ( preference-based indirect feedback ). However, indirect preferential feedback is less efficient in measuring human opinions and requires querying more preferential feedback to model a latent preference function ( González et al., 2017 ; Siivola et al., 2021 ; Nguyen et al., 2021 ) . Additionally, it might suffer from interpretation ambiguity, intransitive and circular preferences (e.g., prefer A over B, and prefer B over C, but prefer C over A, known as rock-paper-scissors relation ), which also presents a challenge for input precision and overall system performance. To overcome the limited number of evaluations at a time and collect more feedback, one can extend pointwise ( n n =1) and pairwise ( n n =2) feedback to listwise ranking ( Cao et al., 2007 ; Siivola et al., 2021 ) ( n > 2 n>2 ), where n n is the number of alternative options. However, many input interface design variations depend on the queried feedback type. Specifically, for direct rating feedback, the listwise approach needs to use n n different rating scales; for indirect preferential feedback, the listwise approach requires a UI to allow users to rank the given outcome alternatives. Despite different queried feedback types, a listwise interface always implicitly facilitates comparisons, as it presents more options simultaneously. Recently, Ou et al. (2023) presented a new approach to overcome current limitations using a n n -alternative ranking approach which provides a “I don’t know” option for signal items. However, the effectiveness is not yet understood. Thus, the main objective of this paper is to understand the following two questions: RQ1 What is the impact of using different opinion measurement interfaces for HITL optimization? RQ2 What is the best-suited interface to use in a HITL optimization to leverage human opinions? Due to the many design choices influencing opinion measurement interfaces, we first derived the design space for opinion measurement interfaces on HITL optimization. We identified six design variations, including pointwise , pairwise , and listwise approaches depending on the type of feedback queried. They can also be varied to support expressing indifference and incomplete preferences. Based on our design space, we conducted an online between-groups study (N=360) to understand the impact of six opinion measurement interfaces on HITL optimization. We selected a text summarization task and an image color enhancement task to evaluate the different opinion measurement interfaces in two domains. In both tasks, humans express their feedback using different user interfaces regarding the quality of text summarization or color enhancement. As a key result, we recommend using a listwise approach and allowing users to express ranking distance to support sequential opinion measurement. This design counterweighs individual ratings and preferential limitations and conveys more direct and effective information for subsequent usage in HITL optimization. The main contribution of this paper is an empirical investigation of how the design of opinion measurement interfaces can influence HITL optimization. We will also discuss design implications and trade-offs for future HITL optimization research and applications.

sections.heading: 2. Related Work
sections.text: In this section, we will discuss the assumptions made when measuring human opinions and how they relate to actual human decisions and preferences. Then, we will discuss how these assumptions could impact modeling human feedback with BO. Lastly, we will revisit the opinion measurement interfaces commonly used today in non-sequential measuring contexts and how existing HITL optimization systems design their opinion measurement interfaces.

sections.heading: 2.1. Assumptions in Human Preferences and Decisions
sections.text: Behaviorism argues that objective decisions and judgments of a human can be observed through their behavior. However, this observation may be limited by the ambiguity of interpretation ( Skinner, 2011 ) due to a lack of observation and impermeable states of mind ( Overgaard, 2006 ) . Opinion measurement is an important complement to behaviorism ( Nobarany et al., 2012 ) . An opinion measurement UI measures “tendencies to evaluate an entity with some degree of favor or disfavor, ordinarily expressed in cognitive, affective, and behavioral responses” ( Eagly and Chaiken, 1993 ) , which reflect human preferences or decisions under uncertainty. Traditional behavioral economics has widely studied rational choice ( Dreier, 1996 ) , and the corresponding algorithmic modeling to infer preferences relied on the transitivity and completeness assumptions. The formulation of transitivity includes two aspects: strict and weak. Strict transitivity states that one choice option is strictly preferred over another, while weak transitivity allows indifference between given choice options. Transitivity as a modeling assumption assumes that people can give consistent ranks to given choice options. However, this assumption may be violated mainly in a sequential judgment context ( Debreu, 1960 ; Bettman et al., 1998 ) since a previous preference may be inverted later in the process and result in a rock-paper-scissors relation due to context changes and cognitive biases ( Tversky and Kahneman, 1974 ) . Moreover, completeness assumes that people always have a preference, but this does not hold for decision-making under uncertain information, where in some cases, the preference may be undecided ( Ok et al., 2012 ) . Identifying the violation of the completeness assumption is more fundamental and complex by definition, as it is harder to define from a behavior perspective. Consequently, violating these assumptions can be framed as preference or decision uncertainty, and it is often strongly assumed that an inverted choice constitutes a noisy observation (e.g., ( González et al., 2017 ; Lin et al., 2022 ; Pfannschmidt et al., 2022 ; Benavoli et al., 2021 ) ) without a detailed inspection from the human perspective.

sections.heading: 2.2. Modeling Human Feedback with Bayesian Optimization
sections.text: Bayesian optimization ( Močkus, 1975 ) is a technique used for the global optimization of expensive-to-evaluate functions. It builds a probabilistic model of the objective function and iteratively selects the next point to evaluate based on an acquisition function that balances exploration and exploitation. The model is updated as new evaluations are made, improving its accuracy over time. Bayesian optimization is beneficial when the objective function is black-box, expensive to evaluate, and multiple local optima exist. It has been successfully applied to various optimization problems in machine learning, engineering, and science ( Shahriari et al., 2016 ) . In addition to engineering aspects, BO can also model human feedback and enables HITL optimization ( Shahriari et al., 2016 ) utilizing, for example, biological measurements ( Kim et al., 2017 ; Ding et al., 2018 ) , interaction behavior ( Chong et al., 2021 ) , and measured preferential choices ( Brochu et al., 2007a ; González et al., 2017 ; Koyama et al., 2017 ) . It learns a posterior from the measured human feedback and aims to search for a global maximum of an unknown function by exploration and exploitation. In conjunction with measured human feedback, two popular genres of BO are actively being researched, as shown in Table 1 . Utility-based BO ( Močkus, 1975 ) requires measuring human feedback as a utility value. In contrast, preference-based BO (PBO) can propose examples using an acquisition function, ask the human to provide a choice, and infer the underlying preference iteratively. Table 1 . Examples of different Bayesian Optimization (BO) frameworks. Types of feedback can be either utility-based or preference-based. Most of the BO frameworks do not model indifference, and none of them consider incomplete preferences. Note that 1) rating can be considered either as absolute utility or preferential ranking distance depending on the underlying preference model, 2) selection is a special case of ranking where one item is strictly preferred over other options, and the ranking order of those unselected options is not specified, which means that their preference relation may be considered incomplete. While BO learns based on absolute utility (e.g., absolute ratings of a given option), PBO learns relative rating or preferential selection as ranking information. To avoid the violations of the transitivity described above, the recent extensions ( Koyama et al., 2020 ; Siivola et al., 2021 ; Benavoli et al., 2021 ) of PBO transited from using a binary pairwise comparison to using a reasonable amount of options, resulting in a listwise comparison. These extensions could largely prevent violations of transitivity and infer more information at a time because they either consider choosing a set of options as winners among all given options ( Koyama et al., 2020 ; Benavoli et al., 2021 ) ; or provide a ranking of all given options, where options may share the same level of rank ( Siivola et al., 2021 ) . Note that more ranking elements may also increase the uncertainty for users and cause them to make imperfect decisions ( Monarch, 2021 ) due to increased workload. Thus, one should carefully consider the presented number of elements. Although PBO has used pairwise comparisons to mitigate various issues regarding unstable human judgment, these current approaches could also violate preference assumptions due to cognitive limitations. Tversky and Kahneman (1974) have widely presented how heuristic biases might influence the choice behavior. External causes can also produce a considerable amount of noisy observations in choice ( Kahneman et al., 2021 ) . To overcome the violation of preference assumptions, PBO has also considered handling noisy inputs ( Letham et al., 2019 ) and guarantees theoretical convergence when dealing with unstable choices. Despite all these developments in PBO, we still observe two challenges in practice. The first is that a human might change their objective during the optimization process, even when using pairwise comparisons. However, PBO assumes a fixed implicit underlying choice function that it can learn. Although PBO can handle noisy input, the other challenge is that it requires much more iterations to let the optimization converge. This is usually very costly when involving a human. We, therefore, need to design the UI carefully to mitigate these challenges and reduce errors.

sections.heading: 2.3. Opinion Measurement Interfaces
sections.text: Figure 2 . Real-world measured opinions in different interfaces: a) Commonly used rating scales to measure opinion regarding one item; b) Two alternative candidates (non-)forced choice; c) Music album song orders without specified criteria, and forced ranking of conferences and movies using a distance. Conventional opinion measurement interfaces have different absolute measures, such as categorical choice and ordinal Likert-scale measures. The underlying analysis is based on Thurstone’s law of comparison ( Thurstone, 1927 ) . The optimal design of a pointwise measuring UI has been explored in psychology to reduce measuring error, for example, by asking repeated questions and checking the overall consistency ( Sherer et al., 1998 ) , regarding the influence of ticks ( Matejka et al., 2016 ) , or by allowing users to express uncertainty about their own input ( Greis et al., 2017 ) . Previous work also discussed improving rating accuracy in the HITL context ( Nguyen et al., 2013 ; Dudley and Kristensson, 2018 ) . A first systematic evaluation regarding the design space was provided by Nobarany et al. (2012) . They also observed that the rating interface might not be ideal for measuring opinions and discussed how to support ranking in the interface. In a way, this is similar to how PBO was designed ( Brochu et al., 2007a ; Brochu et al., 2010 ; González et al., 2017 ) ; opinion measurement interfaces that support comparison were also found beneficial here. Kalloori et al. (2018) discussed a few reasons for better-measured opinions using preference-based feedback: 1) Explicit rating utility suffers from calibration of drift, for concepts with different types of interpretations might lead to differently rated results. 2) Users might change their opinion from time to time due to anchoring ( Payne et al., 1993 ) . 3) Relative questions might potentially be faster and easier to answer. Due to the increased complexity of feedback types, ranking UIs are rarely explored, although there is initial work in this direction ( Luk, 1994 ; Neubarth, 2010 ) .

sections.heading: Interfaces used in the Real World
sections.text: Opinions are frequently measured in real life for a variety of purposes. We can generally observe three genres of these UIs: pointwise, pairwise, and listwise UIs, as shown in Figure 2 .

sections.heading: Interfaces used in HITL Optimization
sections.text: As shown in Figure 3 , many designs for opinion measurement interfaces are used in HITL optimization. Specifically, the presented examples can be treated as a mix of pairwise and listwise comparisons. The underlying feedback type that models the UI’s input form is either utility- or preference-based. Because of this diversity, we will provide a taxonomy to categorize them and determine our study design in the next section. Figure 3 . Examples of opinion measurement interfaces being used in HITL optimizations: a) A user chooses from a list of candidates to optimize illumination ( Marks et al., 1997 ) ; b) A user is asked to choose items that are closer to a given reference ( Wilber et al., 2014 ) ; c) A user is required to decide which of the two given options is closer to their desired material ( Brochu et al., 2007a ) ; d) A user is asked to choose which of two presented texts is more likely to be written on Wikipedia by a human ( Welleck et al., 2020 ) ; e) A user is required to choose which trained machine’s back-flip is better ( Christiano et al., 2017 ) , note that the interface uses a “can’t tell”; f) A user rates four presented graphics animations using a 3-step rating scale to show how close an animation is to what they are looking for ( Brochu et al., 2010 ) ; g) A user rates which of the given paired designs is more preferred ( Koyama et al., 2014 ) ; h) A user must select one target out of a list of choice alternatives ( Koyama et al., 2020 ) . i) A user ranks the given design variations, and each rank position has an associated ordinal rating label ( Ou et al., 2023 ) , and ties are allowed. These interfaces fit in a design space and are discussed in Section 3.1 .

sections.heading: 3. Design Space
sections.text: We revisit the design space of opinion measurement interfaces and extend it to include multiple design variations of the listwise approach. Table 2 provides an overview of the design space of opinion measurement interfaces. The design space formally contains these two dimensions: the number of alternative options and the underlying feedback type . The number of alternative options encodes the complexity when measuring opinion. With more alternative options, we can gather more feedback from a user simultaneously. An interface is pointwise if it only measures the opinion regarding one item. Similarly, interfaces that measure information about two paired items are pairwise . With more than two options, the interface is listwise . For example, in Figure 2 a all interfaces are pointwise as they measure opinions regarding a single instance. Conceptually, a listwise interface also covers interfaces that potentially allow exploring infinite options (n= ∞ \infty , e.g., Koyama et al. (2017) ). However, regardless of the number of options, since a user has to select or mark a subset of preferential relations among all options, e.g., Wilber et al. (2014) , a multiple-item selection can be considered a strict preference between selected and unselected ones. In contrast, the preference order among (un)selected ones remains unspecified. Note that although an interface presents paired options to measure human opinion, it could still ask humans to estimate the distance between two options, which only conveys absolute distance utility as a rating regarding one item to the reference. Furthermore, although Figure 3 f presents four alternatives and asks how close they are to what the user is looking for, this is an absolute rating only concerning the user’s idea of an optimum (which remains unknown to everybody else). These considerations imply that the underlying feedback type, which the framed UI presents as a usage instruction, is also crucial for opinion measurement. The underlying type of feedback can be either utility -based or preference -based. Utility-based interfaces query a human to provide an absolute ordinal or cardinal value regarding an option (the interpretation of the value can differ depending on the context). Preference-based interfaces only measure relative information regarding paired options and, therefore, need further consideration to infer a latent utility. On the one hand, since utility-based interfaces only provide numeric information directly associated with the option, the relative information between options may not be explicit. However, we can sort the utility value. On the other hand, preference-based interfaces only provide local information. A hybrid feedback type provides a subtle design consideration to mix utility- and preference-based information. Similarly, we have two design alternatives, either strict or weak, depending on the type of preference.

sections.heading: 3.1. Applicability
sections.text: We can place the previously presented examples into this design space. Figure 2 a contains 1-RS and n-RS: Twitter and Tinder only utilize binary responses regarding one option (like or not). The Amazon “by feature” rating example is n-RS but evaluates multiple dimensions using scales. In Figure 2 b, there are two examples of 2-AFC or 2-ANFC. Figure 2 c shows three listwise interfaces: n-AFR (songs are ranked without allowing ties and without information about how they are being ranked), n-AFRD (options ranked with a distance, items with the same utility value are forced to be placed on different ranks). Figure 3 a and Figure 3 b are n n -ANFR because they require humans to rank options (permitting ties) without specifying a distance to other options, Figure 3 c and Figure 3 d are 2 2 -AFC because they are judging two options and cannot tell indifference through the UI, Figure 3 e is 2 2 -ANFC because it offers “can’t tell” to its user, Figure 3 f is n n -RS, and Figure 3 g is 1 1 -RS because it is judging how far one item is away from the other, and only judges one option. Figure 3 h is n n -AFR because it selects one out of all options as top-1 ranking. In fact, Figure 3 a and Figure 3 h also use a meaningful 2D layout to present the alternative choices instead of a plain list. While this may improve the efficiency and user experience in specific tasks, it does not change the general structure and, therefore, the classification of the interface. sections.heading: 4. Hypotheses
sections.text: Using this design space, we identified six promising opinion measurement interfaces, i.e., 1-RS, 2-ANFC, n n -RS, n n -AFR, n n -ANFR, n n -ANFRD (UI1 to UI6), see Figure 1 . Our selection is informed by results from related work, which hints that some might be better than others. Thus, we formulate four major hypotheses concerning the performance of HITL optimization when using such an interface:

sections.heading: Hypothesis 1: Baseline
sections.text: Early work on HITL optimizations has shown great performance when using 2-ANFC ( Brochu et al., 2007a ; Brochu et al., 2007b ; Brochu et al., 2010 ) . Their results showed that 2-ANFC systems generally perform better than 1-RS and greatly support HITL systems. We use their initial findings as our baseline comparison and to validate our apparatus. Thus, we hypothesize ( H1 ) that the preference-based interface will outperform the utility-based interface regarding performance measures (UI1 vs. UI2).

sections.heading: Hypothesis 2: Impact of Listwise Approach
sections.text: If H1 is true, this indicates that giving the user more options for comparison will improve the overall system performance. In fact, this is what findings by Cao et al. (2007) suggest. Thus, we hypothesize that a listwise comparison ( n > 2 n>2 ), will outperform comparisons with fewer options. As Listwise is the most flexible in terms of feedback, we next investigate the different strategies that emerged from related work ( Koyama et al., 2017 ; Koyama et al., 2020 ; Mikkola et al., 2020 ) . In this work, we investigate design variations in which the human can either give preferential ratings (e.g., Koyama et al. (2014) ), provide a strict ranking selection (e.g., Koyama et al. (2020) ), a weak ranking selection (e.g., Marks et al. (1997) ), or a combination of those (hybrid). Consequently, we hypothesize ( H2a ) that a listwise interface will outperform a pointwise interface when using utility-based feedback (UI1 vs. UI3). And we hypothesize ( H2b ) that a listwise interface will outperform a pairwise interface when using preference-based feedback (UI2 vs. UI5).

sections.heading: Hypothesis 3: Impact of Listwise Design Variations
sections.text: Based on the initial findings by Mikkola et al. (2020) , we additionally hypothesize H3a and H3b . In detail, we hypothesize H3a that a preference-based listwise ranking interface will outperform a utility-based listwise rating interface (cf. ( Brochu et al., 2007b ; Brochu et al., 2007a ; Brochu et al., 2010 ) ) while allowing for expressing indifference (UI3 vs. UI5). Further, regarding indifference, we hypothesize H3b that being able to express indifference in the interface ( weak preference ) will be better than a forced choice ( strict preference ) (UI4 vs. UI5).

sections.heading: Hypothesis 4: Impact of Hybrid Approach
sections.text: Based on hypotheses H1 - H3 and assuming that their outcome in this work is in line with prior work, Ou et al. (2023) used a new hybrid feedback interface. For this, n-ANFRD (UI6), we pick what we consider to be the best to support the HITL optimization, thus, getting the most information from the user. Thus, we hypothesize that the hybrid listwise interface will outperform: H4a the pairwise interface (UI2), H4b the listwise rating interface (UI3), H4c the listwise strict ranking interface (UI4), and H4d the listwise weak ranking interface (UI5).

sections.heading: 5. User Study
sections.text: We conducted a user study to investigate how different opinion measurement interfaces impact the overall HITL optimization performance to answer our research questions ( RQ1 and RQ2 in Section 1 ) and verify our four hypotheses. Here, we compare the six user interfaces (6 conditions: UI1-UI6, Table 2 and Figure 1 ) using a between-subject design ( Interface ). We used tasks from two domains as a between-subject variable ( Domain ) to shorten the participation time and prevent a learning effect. One group did text summarization tasks from the natural language processing domain. The other group did image color enhancement tasks from the design domain. As dependent variables, we calculated interaction measures from usage logs and feedback from questionnaires (individual rating scales and open questions.)

sections.heading: 5.1. User Interfaces
sections.text: As shown in Figure 1 , we selected six generic interfaces from this design space (1-RS, 2-ANFC, n n -RS, n n -AFR, n n -ANFR, n n -ANFRD) to facilitate our study design better. All interfaces are shown in Figure 4 for both tasks. The following describes the behavior of the six user interfaces: UI1 1-RS uses a bipolar slider-based Likert scale, similar to n n -RS. UI2 2-ANFC uses two radio buttons for preference indication. UI3 n-RS uses a bipolar slider-based Likert scale to indicate the preference for each option. UI4/5 n n -AFR requires a full ranking of all options, and the interface does not allow expressing indifference in this case, whereas n n -ANFR (UI5) can, which characterizes strict and weak preferences. To guarantee a pure ranking behavior in the interface, n n -AFR (UI4), and n n -ANFR (UI5) automatically adjust the distance between options. For example, if a user dropped two boxes on the 1st and 4th choice container box. Then the 4th choice will automatically move up to the 2nd choice and inform users that their ranking is automatically aligned and normalized. UI6 n n -ANFRD is the most flexible listwise ranking interface that permits users to place the option box in any given container box. Additionally, all interfaces include either checkbox options or container boxes to allow users to express incomplete preferences.

sections.heading: 5.2. Task
sections.text: As many applications use HITL optimization, any domain with a set of system parameters to be determined could be used as a HITL optimization task. Examples of such domains are text summarization ( Simpson et al., 2020 ; Ou et al., 2023 ) , image color enhancement ( Koyama et al., 2016 ; Koyama et al., 2017 ; Koyama et al., 2020 ; Ou et al., 2023 ) , melody composition ( Zhou et al., 2021 ) , 3D meshing ( Ou et al., 2022 ; Ou et al., 2023 ) , 3D material design ( Brochu et al., 2007a ) , 3D animation ( Brochu et al., 2010 ) , and 3D illumination ( Marks et al., 1997 ) . In line with previous work ( Ou et al., 2023 ) , we selected text summarization and image color enhancement for the following reasons: First, text and image responses between client and server are easy to handle, lightweight, and fast. Second, the quality of text summarization and image color enhancement is a partly aesthetic judgment, for example, regarding the exact wording and color style. Therefore, it is still challenging to measure this quality objectively ( Bhandari et al., 2020 ; Ou et al., 2023 ) , making it plausible to bring a human into the loop. sections.heading: 5.3. Apparatus
sections.text: We developed the frontend UI1 to UI6 (see Figure 4 and Supplement Video that illustrates the use of all interfaces) using Material UI 1 1 1 https://mui.com/ , last accessed October 10, 2026 and React DnD 2 2 2 https://react-dnd.github.io/react-dnd/about , last accessed October 10, 2026 . We wrote out backend in Go for easier concurrency management. It serves our frontend interfaces, data collection, and communications with other dedicated computing microservices, including two domain services and an optimizer service . We deployed the backend on our institute infrastructure (Ubuntu 20.04, 8-Core Intel Core i9-9900K, 64GB RAM, and NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2080 Ti with 11GB of GPU memory).

sections.heading: 5.3.1. Domain Services: Text Summarization
sections.text: For text summarization, we initially used GPT-3 by OpenAI for text summarization. However, we switched to our self-hosted language model for reproducibility and unlimited quota in the main study. We implemented the backend using Flask and handled text summarization with GPU acceleration. A pressure benchmark shows the backend can handle an average of 6 concurrent requests per second, which determines our rate control to launch parallel participation in our study. We used a pre-trained BART model 3 3 3 https://huggingface.co/sshleifer/distilbart-cnn-12-6 , last accessed October 10, 2026 for text summarization. The model is fine-tuned for CNN daily mail with inference time 307ms, ROUGE-2 score of 21.26, and ROUGE-L score of 30.59, which outperforms a popular baseline ( Lewis et al., 2019 ) . We use Nucleus sampling ( Holtzman et al., 2020 ) as a stochastic text decoding strategy 4 4 4 https://huggingface.co/blog/how-to-generate , last accessed October 10, 2026 for our inference use case because it allows for a bounded parameter space (between 0 and 1) and can generate diverse human-like sentences in the inference phase. Since we designed our user task to consider the length of summarization as a decision criterion, we used a summarization ratio parameter as a hard limit that controls the text generation length and a length penalty parameter as a selected soft limit that encourages the model to generate shorter text. As a result, our hosted text summarization service allows 4 adjustable system parameters at every model inference stage: 1) summarization ratio , 2) length penalty , 3) top-p , and 4) temperature .

sections.heading: 5.3.2. Domain Services: Color Enhancement
sections.text: For image color enhancement, we used a parameterized photo enhancer ( Koyama et al., 2016 ; Koyama et al., 2017 ; Koyama et al., 2020 ) as an image processing service. It allows 5 adjustable system parameters that can range from 0 to 1: 1) brightness , 2) contrast , 3) saturation , 4) temperature , and 5) tint .

sections.heading: 5.3.3. Optimizer Service and Bayesian Optimizers
sections.text: We used Bayesian optimization to give users new options based on their input history. As there is no one Bayesian optimizer to cater to the needs of all six interfaces, we selected the best Bayesian optimizer for each interface. In detail, UI1 and UI3 used naive BO ( Mockus et al., 1978 ) , UI2 used EUBO ( Lin et al., 2022 ) , and UI4-UI6 used the same advanced EUBO. While this could lead to performance differences, we perform benchmark comparisons to ensure they have equal performance; see Appendix A for full details. We used BoTorch ( Balandat et al., 2020 ) to implement all selected optimizers, which reads the user responses to estimate the next optimal system parameters for exploration. The Bayesian optimizer for rating-based interfaces (UI1 and UI3) used the Gaussian process as a surrogate model with Martern 5/2 kernel. The acquisition function is an expected improvement acquisition function that models noisy inputs ( Letham et al., 2019 ) . We used EUBO ( Lin et al., 2022 ) , a BO variate cf. Section 2.2 , as a state-of-the-art PBO optimizer that considers noisy inputs to estimate system parameters for the pairwise interface (UI2). The acquisition function is the Analytic Expected Utility Of Best Option acquisition function ( Lin et al., 2022 ) . The design of the EUBO algorithm guarantees that the current optimum is included in pairwise or listwise comparisons, and we can use the maximum posterior expected utility ( Chu and Ghahramani, 2005 ) to understand the impact on outcome utility. To guarantee fair comparisons and control experiment variables, instead of using different optimizers for all other listwise interfaces (i.e., UI4, UI5, and UI6), we extended EUBO to fit all listwise interfaces 5 5 5 See Supplemental Material for the implementation and further discussions on https://github.com/pytorch/botorch/discussions/1367 , last accessed: October 10, 2026 : We first fit a Gaussian process using the user’s rank data, then use the optimizer learned latent utility f ⁡ ( ⋅ ) f(\cdot) to fit another Gaussian process and infer the next batch of exploration positions. As EUBO maximizes the outcome utility difference between iterations, one can use the utility to analyze the optimization process. Moreover, in UI2 and UI4-UI6, although EUBO does not assume noiseless observations, we discarded indifference and incomplete preference input instead of generating a random preference order as 1) EUBO does not model indifference, 2) providing noisy input can decrease optimization performance and make a strong assumption about the preference model. These three Bayesian optimizers can optimize for our objectives and outperform pure random exploration in various simulated tasks, see Appendix A for comparisons. Figure 5 . The study procedure. Each participant completed three news articles or three photos, and each task item underwent at least 4 initial iterations for exploring the participant’s preference prior.

sections.heading: 5.4. Procedure
sections.text: The overall procedure for the participants is visualized in Figure 5 . Participants started the study with an informed consent form and answered initial demographic questions, including their age, gender, and levels of language proficiency. The opinion measurement interface then presents a set of evaluation options to the participants. The main task is to provide feedback, using the UI, to the AI to summarize the given news articles as much as possible while preserving the meaning of the article or enhance the image color as much as possible according to the preferences of the participants . Because the optimizers need initialization samples, in the first 4 iterations, a participant evaluated outcomes produced by quasi-random Sobol sampled ( Rezende et al., 2014 ; Wilson et al., 2017 ) system parameters. After acquiring these preference priors from participants, starting from the 5th iteration, the optimizer is used, and participants can freely terminate when satisfied with the current system outcomes. The task ends automatically after 20 iterations to limit participation time. After termination, participants answered six questions about their satisfaction with the system outcomes and their experience using the interface to provide feedback. Each participant completed three Latin square-shuffled 1) news articles selected from the CNN daily mail 6 6 6 https://huggingface.co/datasets/cnn_dailymail , last accessed October 10, 2026 dataset, which covered topics of sports, politics, and entertainment 7 7 7 Article IDs: ea06fd0b25cb9793397a, 35f0e33de7923036a97a, 42c027e4ff9730fbb3de , or 2) photos 8 8 8 https://github.com/yuki-koyama/sequential-gallery/tree/main/resources/scaled , last accessed October 10, 2026 selected from the Sequential Gallery by Koyama et al. (2020) .

sections.heading: 5.5. Participants
sections.text: We recruited participants worldwide via Prolific. Because participants had different median completion times in different experimental conditions, we paid between £3 to £9 upon completion, corresponding to an hourly wage of £9/h. Participation was under informed consent, and the study adhered to the European General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). In total, we collected data from 635 participants from 25 countries. To guarantee high-quality responses, we only consider participants if they: 1) had an approval rate of 95%, 2) completed the study only once, 3) answered with consistent demographics, e.g., not more than five years of age difference in the study compared to the platform registration information, and 4) provided their response in at least a reasonable amount of time, i.e., spent longer than 3 seconds in each iteration to read the summarized text, longer than 1 second in each iteration to check the image and interact with the interface according to our pilot study observations. Therefore, we will report our results based on 360 participants (171 female, 185 male, and 4 diverse; age μ = 28.14 , σ = 8.39 \mu=28.14,\sigma=8.39 , range 18-66), with varied self-indicated English proficiency (CEFR scale 9 9 9 CEFR scale: https://www.coe.int/en/web/common-european-framework-reference-languages/table-1-cefr-3.3-common-reference-levels-global-scale , last accessed October 10, 2026 : A1 0.55%, A2 0.55%, B1 3.89%, B2 21.67%, C1 43.33%, C2 30.00%) and varied self-indicated image color enhancement expertise (None 12.2%, Novice 46.7%, Intermediate 30.0%, Experienced 10.6%, Expert 0.6%). We tested the six Interfaces with 30 participants per Domain ( Text Summarization and Image Color Enhancement ).

sections.heading: 5.6. Performance Indicators and Measurements
sections.text: A high-performance HITL optimization loop is considered successful from the human side when the human spends less time on providing feedback, can achieve a satisfactory result in fewer iterations, and the interface allows the human to give more precise and clear feedback. From the machine side, the underlying optimizer can learn human feedback more effectively and propose outcomes of high objective quality faster. Therefore, we measured participants’ interaction details in each interface as behavior measures . Next, we recorded participants’ provided feedback and corresponding system outcomes as feedback measures for the optimization loop. Lastly, we measured users’ subjective experience with the system after each completion as questionnaire measures .

sections.heading: 5.6.1. Behavior Measures
sections.text: We measured the participants’ interaction in each interface using six measurements. 1) Decision Time per Iteration , measured from when the evaluation options were presented to the last time when participants interacted with the interface, 2) Decision Time per Item , the Decision Time per Iteration divided by the number of items shown, 3) number of iterations per task, 4) Number of Ranking Interactions , the number of operations to rank the given system outcomes in listwise interfaces, 5) Number of Indifferent Preference , number of pairs that are rated the same, and 6) Number of Incomplete Preference counted as the number of times the “I don’t know” option was ticked per task.

sections.heading: 5.6.2. Feedback Measures
sections.text: To evaluate the optimization loop on the human side, we collected participants’ rating and preferential ranking data in each iteration. Here, we used the normalized number of iterations as Progress over the course of the HITL optimization. Moreover, we quantify human feedback using the user feedback from direct rating (UI1, UI3, and UI6 10 10 10 The ranking distance labels in UI6 are mapped to utility accordingly, e.g., 0 for Terrible and 100 for Excellent . ) or the optimizer learned latent utility from preferential rankings (UI2, UI4, UI5, and UI6). The learned latent utility is a Laplace approximation of the posterior mean of the estimated utility values ( Chu and Ghahramani, 2005 ) . As EUBO maximizes the posterior expected utility ( Lin et al., 2022 ) , it represents the estimated user feedback when the query is chosen in the input space based on the available data and the current Gaussian process model. By comparing the posterior mean values at different iterations, we can gain insights into how the optimizer performs and whether it converges toward the user’s expected solution. On the machine side, we computed the Length of the text, the ROUGE ( ROUGE-1 , ROUGE-2 , and ROUGE-L ) ( Lin, 2004 ) , and BLEU ( Papineni et al., 2002 ) scores for the optimized text summarization to measure the objective quality of summarized texts as they correlate positively with human evaluation. Ou et al. (2023) used the exact same measures in their HITL text summarization task. ROUGE measures how many human-summarized words appear in the machine-generated summaries, and BLEU measures precision regarding how many words in the machine-generated words appear in the human reference summaries. For the image color enhancement, we computed Saturation , Contrast , and Brightness using a mean of pixel-wise subtraction between source and outcome in the H, S, and V channels correspondingly. Furthermore, we computed the mean pixel-wise difference of U channels in YUV color space for Tint changes and similarly in the V channel for Temperature changes. These five measures are also in line with prior work by Ou et al. (2023) . Note: While the computed quality metrics are not true measurements of quality per se, together with the strategy of the optimizer to always show the current best choice, a consistent trend here can be seen as an indication of continued improvements and considered a successful optimization if at least one measured objective is being improved. Thus, we measure the semantic meaning of text summarization and only compare it to one human writer’s ground truth, provided in the CNN daily mail dataset. Similarly, the color metrics only correlate to human judgment and do not measure individual color preferences. Although those metrics stay technical, they positively correlate with human judgment.

sections.heading: 5.6.3. Questionnaire Measures
sections.text: In line with work by Ou et al. (2023) , we asked six questions to obtain 100-point bipolar Likert scale responses for robust input ( Funke and Reips, 2012 ) without ticks to prevent biases ( Matejka et al., 2016 ) . Q1) I strongly agree the final result matches my expectation of the results ; Q2) I firmly believe I can do better a result alone than this AI ; Q3) I am strongly satisfied with the final result ; Q4) I strongly believe the AI indeed improved the result based on my feedback. ; Q5) I think the “I don’t know” option helped me to express my feedback to the AI more precisely , and Q6) I believe I had given clear feedback to the AI . Here, Ou et al. (2023) showed that Q1-Q4 have a high correlation and therefore used the aggregated value as an indicator for Satisfaction . Q5 indicates whether expressing “I don’t know” was considered helpful, and Q6 indicates whether users think that the UI can give feedback clearly. Lastly, we obtained open-ended responses from participants with the instruction “ Describe your experience while working with this AI. ”

sections.heading: 6. Results
sections.text: In this section, we first present participants’ behavior regarding interface interactions, including their total iterations, decision time per iteration, and how they express indifference and incomplete preferences. Then, we show the effectiveness of the feedback optimization loop regarding the objective quality and feedback utility. Finally, we present subjective responses and comments from the questionnaire. Since our hypotheses H1 and H2 in Section 4 compare two UIs, we analyze normally distributed data using a t-test or a Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test in case the Shapiro-Wilk test ( Razali et al., 2011 ) indicates that the normality is violated. We use linear mixed models (LMMs) ( Bates et al., 2014 ; Kuznetsova et al., 2017 ) for H3 and H4 to report our results and to quantify the optimization loop statistically. The models include participants as a random effect and compare pairwise and listwise UIs between groups. For non-significant independent two-sample tests, we conduct either a Bayesian independent t-test or a Bayesian Mann-Whitney test and analyze the Bayes Factor ( Wagenmakers, 2007 ; Rouder et al., 2009 ) to quantify the likelihood of hypotheses. The full results are available from reproducible scripts in supplemental materials: https://github.com/changkun/rankui .

sections.heading: 6.1.1. Decision Time per Iteration
sections.text: For H1 , for decision time per iteration, we found no significant difference between UI1 and UI2 in text summarization, but UI1 caused a significant increase in decision time compared to UI2 in image color enhancement, see Figure 6 and Table 3 . Regarding average decision time per item, there is a significant difference between UI1 and UI2. This means that providing comparisons enables faster decisions. For H2 , UI3 results in a significantly longer decision time per iteration than UI1, and UI5 has a significantly longer decision time per iteration than UI2, which is true for both domains. This indicates that users need more decision time to judge more given options .

sections.heading: 6.1.2. Decision Time per Item
sections.text: However, when checking decision time per item, UI1 takes significantly more time than UI3 in both domains, while we found no significant difference between UI2 and UI5. This indicates that the listwise approach did not increase decision time per item. Finally, we fitted general linear mixed models for H3 and H4 using the Gamma family with an inverse link ( Lo and Andrews, 2015 ) . None showed significant differences in UI3-UI6 regarding decision time, except H4a : It compares UI2 to UI6, and the effect of UI2 is statistically significant and positive regarding decision time per iteration. Although the pairwise interface enables faster total decision time when there are more options, it does not make per-item decisions significantly faster than the listwise approach.

sections.heading: 6.1.3. Interaction Behavior – Number of Iterations
sections.text: For the total iterations, we found that participants explored significantly more with UI1 than with UI2 ( H1 ) and UI3 ( H2a ) in both domains, see Figure 6 and Table 3 . However, we found no significant differences between UI2 and UI3 ( H2b ). We fitted Poisson mixed models for H3 and H4 , and in total iterations, there were no significant differences for most of the comparisons between pairwise and listwise interfaces (UI2-UI6) in both domains. While the pointwise interface (UI1) resulted in significantly more iterations than the other interfaces, there were no significant differences across domains between pairwise and listwise interfaces (UI2-UI6).

sections.heading: 6.1.4. Interaction Behavior – Number of Ranking Interactions
sections.text: We recorded the ranking interaction from UI4 to UI6 for H4 , see Figure 6 . In text summarization, a fitted Poisson mixed model showed that compared to the total ranking interactions in UI6 ( β \beta =1.627, SE=0.023, t=69.873, p<.001), the effect for UI4 is statistically significant and positive ( β \beta =0.065, SE=0.033, t=1.986, p=.047). For UI5, the effect is statistically non-significant and positive ( β \beta =0.037, SE=0.032, t=1.156, p=.248). However, in image color enhancement, compared to the total ranking interactions in UI6 ( β \beta =4.700, SE=0.064, t=73.761, p < .001), the effects for UI4 ( β \beta =-0.001, SE=0.092, t=-0.008, p=.994) and UI5 ( β \beta =-0.001, SE=.092, t=-.008, p=.479) are both statistically non-significant. In sum, we found that with the same BO optimizer under the hood, participants tend to produce fewer ranking interactions with UI6 than with other listwise interfaces (UI4 and UI5).

sections.heading: 6.1.5. Preference Type – Expressing Indifference
sections.text: Following our study design, UI1 and UI4 cannot express indifference for indifference preference. Thus, we do not evaluate H2a and H3b here. We found that UI5 prompted participants to express significantly more indifference preference than UI2 ( H2b ) for preference-based feedback; see Figure 6 and Table 3 . However, we found no significant difference between UI3 and UI5 for expressing indifference preference. We fitted Poisson mixed models for H4a , H4b , and H4d , comparing them to UI6, see Figure 6 and Table 3 . The effect of UI3 is statistically significant and negative compared to UI6. The effect of UI5 is statistically significant and negative. These results apply to both domains we studied. Hence, compared to all other UIs, participants express indifference significantly more often when using UI6 .

sections.heading: 6.1.6. Preference Type – Expressing Incompleteness
sections.text: We first inspected the Wilcoxon signed rank test for participants who moved their sliders and used the “I don’t know” checkbox in UI1 and UI4 because these interfaces cannot express indifference preference. We found no significant difference between adjusting the slider to the midpoint and clicking “I don’t know” (W = 239.50, p = .219; r = -0.24, C ​ I 95 % = [ − 0.55 , 0.13 ] , B ​ F 10 = 0.638 CI_{95\%}=[-0.55,0.13],BF_{10}=0.638 ). This result verifies the prior work regarding the indifference between incomplete preference and midpoint rating ( Armstrong, 1987 ) in a bipolar Likert scale and validates our apparatus. In text summarization, for H1 , participants with UI2 did not express significantly more incomplete preferences than with UI1, similar when comparing UI1 vs. UI3 ( H2a ), and UI2 vs. UI5 ( H2b ), see Figure 6 and Table 3 . For H3 , a fitted Poisson mixed model shows when compared to UI5, UI3 is statistically non-significant and positive, but the effect of UI4 is statistically significant and positive. Another fitted Poisson mixed model for H4 shows that, compared to UI6, only UI4 is statistically significant and positive. Similarly, in image color enhancement, results showed that UI6 is expressed significantly less than UI2, UI4, and UI5. Therefore, compared to all other UIs, participants tend to express fewer incomplete preferences when using UI6.

sections.heading: 6.2. The Optimization Loop
sections.text: The overall optimization loop produces three types of data: 1) the optimized system outcomes, 2) user feedback (either absolute ratings or preferential rankings), and 3) an optimizer-inferred (latent) utility function. To analyze the optimization loop, we selected a similar approach that analyzes the stationarity of rating responses ( Ou et al., 2022 ) and the optimizer predictions ( Ou et al., 2023 ) : in a successful optimization loop, the system outcomes should align and come closer to user expectations over iterations based on user feedback. Otherwise, the system outcomes should go back and forth or further away from user expectations. As a result, to compare how the optimization loops work differently in different UIs, we should expect to observe: 1) The objective quality (see Section 5.6.2 for the selected metrics) of optimized system outcomes progress significantly in at least one objective. 2) User feedback should give higher utility responses progressively. 3) Optimizer learned latent utility (see Section 5.3.3 ) increases progressively.

sections.heading: 6.2.2. User Feedback and Optimizer Learned Utility of Preferences
sections.text: When using UI1 and UI3, we asked users to provide absolute ratings of system-generated solutions (for utility-based optimizers), which we consider a user feedback . In contrast, in UI2, UI4, and UI5, users provide ranking responses (for preference-based optimizers) that give local preference relations between system outcomes. Based on this, the Bayesian optimizers then infer the learned latent utility . Lastly, in UI6, as it mixes absolute ratings and rankings, we can analyze both user feedback and the learned latent utility . We specify the construction of the measure in Section 5.6.2 . Thus, we can use either the user feedback or the learned latent utility to compare the optimization progress between UIs. In total, we use four LMMs to compare the different UIs using either user feedback or lerned latent utility as dependent variables. Therefore, we fitted four LMMs regarding user feedback and lerned latent utility independently from the Domain . We used Interface and Progress as fixed main effects to compare the performance between UIs; see Figure 8 , Figure 9 , and Table 4 . First, we investigate the user feedback in both domains. For the text summarization domain, the LMM results showed the effect of iteration is statistically significant and positive, and UI6 outperforms UI1 and UI3; see “User feedback” in Table 4 . For the image color enhancement domain, the results show that UI6 significantly outperforms the other UIs. Second, we investigate the learned latent utility in both domains. The results of the LMM for the text summarization domain showed the effect of iteration is statistically non-significant and negative. However, UI6 is significantly better than UI2, UI4, and UI5. For the image color enhancement domain, UI6 significantly outperforms the other UIs. In summary, UI6 significantly outperforms the other UIs regarding optimizer lerned latent utility and user feedback . These results show that through HITL optimizations, UI6 produced significantly higher utility than all other interfaces (UI1-UI5) in both domains . sections.heading: 7. Discussion
sections.text: Overall, we found significant differences in that all other interfaces outperform the pointwise interfaces in both studied domains. Still, there are subtle differences between the list- and pair-wise user interfaces. In this section, we structure the results according to our initial hypotheses and summarize possible implications and trade-offs when determining the use of an interface for HITL optimization.

sections.heading: H1: Baseline Apparatus Verification
sections.text: Based on our results, the 2-ANFC pairwise interface (UI2) outperforms the 1-RS pointwise interface (UI1) because it has a significantly lower decision time per item and fewer iterations. The 2-ANFC also helped participants to express indifference and their incomplete preference for better system parameter exploration and exploitation. Participants using 2-ANFC also reported significantly higher satisfaction compared to 1-RS. This result verifies that our apparatus is valid and aligns with discussions in prior work ( Brochu et al., 2007a ; Brochu et al., 2007b ; Brochu et al., 2010 ) .

sections.heading: H2: The Listwise Approach
sections.text: In terms of UI interactions, our results showed that listwise interfaces ( n n -RS/ n n -ANFR, UI3/UI5) provide the following advantages (compared to 1-RS/2-ANFC, UI1/UI2): 1) they allow users to evaluate more options without increasing decision time and iterations; 2) users express more indifferent preferences and less incomplete preferences; 3) they allow implicit comparisons among all given options. However, the direct use of the listwise approach (i.e., using more sliders to rate more items than 1-RS or rank multiple items without distance in n n -ANFR) did not significantly improve the performance of the optimization loop.

sections.heading: H3: Design Variations of The Listwise Approach
sections.text: When comparing design variations regarding querying different feedback types for ranking ( H3a : n n -RS vs. n n -ANFR, i.e., UI3 vs. UI5), allowing expressing indifference and incomplete preferences ( H3b : n n -AFR vs. n n -ANFR, i.e., UI4 vs. UI5) in listwise approach, we did not find enough evidence to show a difference in decision time, involved iterations, and the performance of the optimization loop. The subjectively reported satisfaction also did not differ significantly from each other. However, n n -AFR expresses significantly more incomplete preferences compared to n n -ANFR.

sections.heading: H4: The Hybrid Approach
sections.text: We found that the hybrid approach ( n n -ANFRD, UI6) did not differ from 2-ANFC ( H4a ), n n -RS ( H4b ), n n -AFR ( H4c ), n n -ANFR ( H4d ) in terms of decision time per item and involved iterations, and subjective satisfaction. However, n n -ANFR lets participants express indifference significantly more than other interfaces, resulting in fewer ranking interactions. When checking the performance of the optimization loop, n n -ANFRD showed significantly higher user input utility throughout the loop and higher latent preferent utility compared to pairwise and other listwise interfaces.

sections.heading: 7.2. Interpretation and Implications
sections.text: While we initially assumed using a listwise approach that increased the number of parallel comparisons could improve the overall performance, the results did not support this assumption, particularly for acquired decision time. Based on the validation of H3 , neither n n -RS (UI3, utility-based) nor n n -ANFR (UI5, preference-based) show a significant advantage and only increased the overall decision time in the loop compared to 2-ANFC (UI2, preference-based). This might be because neither n n -RS nor n n -ANFR provided enough support for participants to reduce the overall noisy observations, and there is room for improvement when using a BO optimizer specifically designed for listwise UIs. In n n -RS, despite multiple given alternatives, participants might not notice the relative position between different sliders; in n n -ANFR, the UI did not demonstrate enough absolute cues to participants on how pure ranking can influence their input, and a pure local ranking may not give participants information on a global overview. Instead, the n n -ANFRD (UI6) hybrids collect utility-based and preference-based feedback by providing rating scales in the regular listwise ranking UI. Similar to other listwise UIs, based on the validation of H4 , although n n -ANFRD increased total decision time, our results show the general advantage of preference elicitation (expressing more indifference, fewer ranking interactions, fewer incomplete preferences, and better performance in the optimization loop). This could be interpreted as the UI starting to offer participants implicit recall support for their past ratings if their ranking positions are improving. In addition, n n -ANFRD resulted in fewer ranking interactions and made it clearer for participants to express a ranking decision compared to other purely listwise ranking interfaces. Furthermore, our results regarding designing UIs to support indifference and incomplete preferences offer implications for future modeling algorithms. In Bayesian optimization, indifference preference behavior could be an indicator to inform the acquisition function to avoid exploiting these areas; incomplete preferences might be another indicator to balance exploration and exploitation. Depending on the context, one might design the algorithm to a) avoid exploring a space where people had an incomplete preference to reduce input uncertainty, or alternatively b) explore it even more for creativity support and then integrate the measured preferences with more interaction behavior, such as interface features and task completion time ( Dudley et al., 2019 ) , to better support the optimization process.

sections.heading: 7.3. Design Trade-Offs
sections.text: As we validated in our hypotheses, there are many subtle differences between pairwise and listwise interfaces when permitting users to express indifference and incomplete preferences. This gives us evidence of how they could impact HITL optimization performance. Below, we discuss potential trade-offs when using these interfaces.

sections.heading: 7.3.1. Guideline 1: Pointwise Approach
sections.text: The pointwise slider-based interface has proven useful in many disciplines, such as psychology, subjective scale measures, etc. It is useful to identify social agreement among populations and measure the direct utility given by a human. The technique for processing these types of data is also mature. But it is precarious and problematic when directly applying it to individual sequential measurements. Future HITL optimization systems or any sequential measurement should generally avoid using this approach.

sections.heading: 7.3.2. Guideline 2: Pairwise Approach
sections.text: A pairwise interface only requires a human to judge based on the comparison of two given items. Since there is no measured utility and it only provides relative information about two items, the modeling of the latent utility function could suffer from a change of criteria and intransitive preference when the anchoring point between two sessions is not chosen properly. When an iteration receives an incomplete preference, the underlying optimizer could not receive much useful modeling information. However, when a design objective is to optimize for fast decisions, the pairwise approach (2-ANFC) is a winner among alternative listwise designs.

sections.heading: 7.3.3. Guideline 3: Listwise Approach
sections.text: Listwise interfaces establish a comparison by increasing the number of alternatives. Similar to the pairwise interface, a listwise interface without measuring ranking distance ( n n -AFR and n n -ANFR in our study) requires a properly sampled anchoring option between iterations to establish a ranking function. Otherwise, there is no direct association between iterations. Instead, a listwise interface that allows expressing ranking distance ( n n -RS and n n -ANFRD in our study) conveys an implicit association between different iterations regardless of whether the human provides local or global judgments it is more suited to use in a HITL optimization context. Furthermore, n n -ANFRD is better than n n -RS because a concentrated participant may not notice the relative slider position between parallel judging options in n n -RS, but n n -ANFRD explicitly visualizes the ranking in the UI for users, which helps users more clearly express their opinion in a sequential task. As design suggestions, when there is a limited measuring budget, e.g., one can only query humans for a very limited number of opinions, applying listwise interfaces is considered better than pairwise because it provides more measurement of their opinion and does not decrease the optimization performance. Furthermore, allowing users to express the ranking distance ( n n -ANFRD) is the winner of all listwise variations ( n n -RS, n n -AFR, and n n -ANFR).

sections.heading: 7.3.4. Guideline 4: Measuring Indifference and Incomplete Preferences
sections.text: When measuring more accurate user opinions, allowing them to express indifference and incomplete preferences is crucial. For the pointwise interface, these two different types of preference were implicitly ignored and treated as being indicated by centering the slider. This interpretation of a central slider position may be true with proper task wording. Still, it may be easily misused and produce more noisy input when a user does not know how to express their opinion with the interface. Therefore, in the HITL optimization scenario, it is better to explicitly design these two functionalities to support users in expressing their indifference and incomplete preferences. This information could also inform optimizers to avoid exploring these areas. This is particularly important when the evaluation budget is very limited in the HITL optimization context.

sections.heading: 7.4. Limitations and Future Work
sections.text: Our study used a text summarization task and an image color enhancement task to explore the impact of interfaces in HITL optimization. While these domains are common and make it easy to run a study online at scale, we did not verify our results on more domains. Although we did not find a large difference between the text and image domains, the same study paradigm could be evaluated in other domains, such as the 3D domain, where visual decisions are harder to make due to the complexity of geometry, which may result in different observed behaviors. This might be interesting for future investigation. Since our optimization context is highly dependent on humans and modeled human feedback as objective functions, the system performance highly depends on the quality of human input. The responses collected online may be influenced by participants’ environments, such as slow decision time due to external distractions. Moreover, for the preferential settings, depending on the underlying optimizer (e.g., Brochu et al. (2007a) ), the decision time might be different if the system repeatedly returns the current optimum. Our study evaluated opinion measurement interfaces, not optimizers. However, differently designed listwise interfaces could benefit from dedicated Bayesian optimizers. Without a specialized BO optimizer, our suggested n n -ANFRD interface supports the user to express a ranking distance and still outperforms other interfaces in various aspects, such as fewer ranking interactions, more clearly stated indifference, and rarely expressed incomplete preferences. We also did not look into a detailed inspection of the cause of indifference and incomplete preference. This leaves a large potential for 1) future HCI research to study factors, such as involved expertise, and 2) future BO algorithmic research to model the influence of different optimizers on the same interface, the interaction effects between interfaces and optimizers, and more realistic modeling of indifference and incomplete preference. Lastly, we focused on the design space for aggregated preferences and used Bayesian optimizers that assumed one latent preference function. However, this could be limited by the human preference aggregation process, where multiple criteria may not be expressed simultaneously. Future work can extend the design space to multi-criteria opinion measurement interfaces and further exploit multi-objective Bayesian optimization methods ( Benavoli et al., 2021 ; Daulton et al., 2020 ) . Similarly, our discussed taxonomy and design space only considered structured measures. Hence, we did not explore UIs that utilize unstructured input, such as text prompts ( Dang et al., 2022 ) and human-sketched edits ( Chong et al., 2021 ) of generative models.

sections.heading: 8. Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we revisited the design space of opinion measurement interfaces in the HITL optimization context. Concretely, we aimed to determine the best-suited interface to query human judgments in sequential evaluation. We found subtle differences between pairwise opinion measurement interfaces and listwise ones: In particular, listwise interfaces helped users express more indifference preferences over incomplete preferences than the pairwise interface. Moreover, the hybrid interface that mixes the utility-based and preferential ranking-based feedback to counterbalance the limitations of each approach could better emphasize the relative relation of options for users and achieve better HITL optimization performance. As winners, both n n -ANFRD and 2-ANFC have unique advantages. The design decision between them is a trade-off of decision time, the precision of measured human feedback, and overall optimization loop performance. Looking ahead, the exploration of interface designs for HITL optimization does not end here: Our considered design space only covers structured human inputs bound to suitable optimizers, i.e., utility and preferential data. With the increasing developments in large language models, it would also be interesting and challenging to explore, quantify, and evaluate human-in-the-loop interfaces that allow unstructured inputs such as using a text prompt ( Dang et al., 2022 ) to alter media data using diffusion models ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) . Our results here provide a starting point in this direction.

sections.text: Figure 11 . The performance benchmark for validating our implemented Bayesian optimizers (for different UIs) compares to a random exploration (baseline). Higher y-axis utility values mean better exploitation performance. The upper row shows exploitation performance using a random sampler for the initial samples. The bottom row shows exploitation performance using a Sobol sampler. Each column shows the performance of a different synthetic function. The results validate our implemented BOs and outperform random exploration. As described in Section 5.3.3 , for utility-based UIs ( 1 1 -RS/ n n -RS, UI1/UI3), we implemented a utility-based BO; for preference-based UIs, we use EUBO ( Lin et al., 2022 ) that is designed for pairwise comparisons ( 2 2 -ANFC, UI2); but also for all listwise interfaces ( n n -AFC/ n n -ANFC/ n n -ANFCD, UI4/UI5/UI6), to not introduce another experiment variable. We adopted EUBO so that the optimizer can infer a batch of outcomes based on ranking preferences. To demonstrate the validity of our implemented Bayesian optimizer, we selected four standard synthetic functions 11 11 11 See https://www.sfu.ca/~ssurjano/optimization.html for exact definitions, last accessed October 10, 2026 : Weighted Vector Sum (5D), Hartmann (6D), Levy (10D), and Ackley (20D) for the benchmarks. The results in Figure 11 demonstrate that all of our implemented Bayesian optimizers outperform random exploration. Full implementation details can be found in the supplemental material.
