Different opinion measurement interfaces: UI1) Single item Rating Scale (1-RS); UI2) Two Alternative Non-Forced Choice (2-ANFC); UI3) n n -items Rating Scales ( n n -RS); UI4) n n -Alternative Forced Ranking ( n n -AFR); UI5) n n -Alternative Non-Forced Ranking ( n n -ANFR); UI6) n n -Alternative Non-Forced Ranking with Distance ( n n -ANFRD). The 1-RS and n n -RS interfaces are rating scale-based measurements, and the 2-ANFC, n n -AFR, and n n -ANFR are preference-based ranking interfaces. As a combination, the n n -ANFRD mixes absolute ratings and preferential rankings, which permits expressing not only ranking orders but also local ordinal ranking distance. All interfaces in this gallery also permit users to express their incomplete preference through “I don’t know,” and to signal when a satisfactory result is achieved through “I’m satisfied.” Abstract. Human-in-the-loop optimization refers to systems that present choices to a human decision-maker and query their judgment to optimize system parameters iteratively. The user interface typically provides either an absolute rating scale or asks for a preferred option. However, these approaches can potentially suffer from calibration problems, inconsistencies, and completeness violations of user preferences in such a sequential evaluation. This paper revisits the design space of opinion measurement interfaces for human-in-the-loop optimization. We conducted a study (N=360) using text summarization and image color enhancement tasks to evaluate human sequential feedback in six representative opinion measurement interfaces. Based on our analysis, we recommend using a listwise approach to support sequential opinion measurement, which counterweighs individual rating and preferential choice limitations and conveys more information for subsequent use. We further discuss the trade-offs in different user interface designs and provide guidelines to inform future research. Keywords: human-in-the-loop machine learning; adaptive human-computer interaction; opinion measurement interface; design guidelines 1. Introduction Human-in-the-loop ( Monarch, 2021 ) (HITL) optimization has received increasing attention in HCI ( Zhou et al., 2021 ; Chan et al., 2022 ) . Such systems query decision makers for their judgment among machine proposals, e.g., using Bayesian optimization (BO) ( Kushner, 1964 ; Shahriari et al., 2016 ) as the background AI and then optimize underlying system parameters toward user preferences according to the feedback. One of the benefits is that this adaptation can support users to explore a design space ( Koyama et al., 2020 ; Yue et al., 2021 ; Chan et al., 2022 ) defined by finite criteria or retain more control over pre-configured system decision strategies ( Russell, 2019 ) . However, the opinion measurement interface ( Nobarany et al., 2012 ) used as input component in HITL optimization has many design parameters itself. Depending on the types of human feedback required, the whole process has different limitations due to the design of the input interface. For example, a commonly used pointwise user interface (UI) asks the user to rate a given option as utility-based direct feedback , see Figure 2 a. Although, literature has shown that humans are not good at absolute judgments ( Tversky and Kahneman, 1974 ) and tend to give local judgments ( Brochu et al., 2007a ) . Therefore, a rating interface could suffer from miscalibration and noisy human feedback, thus reducing human-AI cooperation performance. Another popular pairwise design ( Brochu et al., 2007a ; Christiano et al., 2017 ) is to ask humans which of the two given system outcomes is preferred ( preference-based indirect feedback ). However, indirect preferential feedback is less efficient in measuring human opinions and requires querying more preferential feedback to model a latent preference function ( González et al., 2017 ; Siivola et al., 2021 ; Nguyen et al., 2021 ) . Additionally, it might suffer from interpretation ambiguity, intransitive and circular preferences (e.g., prefer A over B, and prefer B over C, but prefer C over A, known as rock-paper-scissors relation ), which also presents a challenge for input precision and overall system performance. To overcome the limited number of evaluations at a time and collect more feedback, one can extend pointwise ( n n =1) and pairwise ( n n =2) feedback to listwise ranking ( Cao et al., 2007 ; Siivola et al., 2021 ) ( n > 2 n>2 ), where n n is the number of alternative options. However, many input interface design variations depend on the queried feedback type. Specifically, for direct rating feedback, the listwise approach needs to use n n different rating scales; for indirect preferential feedback, the listwise approach requires a UI to allow users to rank the given outcome alternatives. Despite different queried feedback types, a listwise interface always implicitly facilitates comparisons, as it presents more options simultaneously. Recently, Ou et al. (2023) presented a new approach to overcome current limitations using a n n -alternative ranking approach which provides a “I don’t know” option for signal items. However, the effectiveness is not yet understood. Thus, the main objective of this paper is to understand the following two questions: RQ1 What is the impact of using different opinion measurement interfaces for HITL optimization? RQ2 What is the best-suited interface to use in a HITL optimization to leverage human opinions? Due to the many design choices influencing opinion measurement interfaces, we first derived the design space for opinion measurement interfaces on HITL optimization. We identified six design variations, including pointwise , pairwise , and listwise approaches depending on the type of feedback queried. They can also be varied to support expressing indifference and incomplete preferences. Based on our design space, we conducted an online between-groups study (N=360) to understand the impact of six opinion measurement interfaces on HITL optimization. We selected a text summarization task and an image color enhancement task to evaluate the different opinion measurement interfaces in two domains. In both tasks, humans express their feedback using different user interfaces regarding the quality of text summarization or color enhancement. As a key result, we recommend using a listwise approach and allowing users to express ranking distance to support sequential opinion measurement. This design counterweighs individual ratings and preferential limitations and conveys more direct and effective information for subsequent usage in HITL optimization. The main contribution of this paper is an empirical investigation of how the design of opinion measurement interfaces can influence HITL optimization. We will also discuss design implications and trade-offs for future HITL optimization research and applications. 2. Related Work In this section, we will discuss the assumptions made when measuring human opinions and how they relate to actual human decisions and preferences. Then, we will discuss how these assumptions could impact modeling human feedback with BO. Lastly, we will revisit the opinion measurement interfaces commonly used today in non-sequential measuring contexts and how existing HITL optimization systems design their opinion measurement interfaces. 2.1. Assumptions in Human Preferences and Decisions Behaviorism argues that objective decisions and judgments of a human can be observed through their behavior. However, this observation may be limited by the ambiguity of interpretation ( Skinner, 2011 ) due to a lack of observation and impermeable states of mind ( Overgaard, 2006 ) . Opinion measurement is an important complement to behaviorism ( Nobarany et al., 2012 ) . An opinion measurement UI measures “tendencies to evaluate an entity with some degree of favor or disfavor, ordinarily expressed in cognitive, affective, and behavioral responses” ( Eagly and Chaiken, 1993 ) , which reflect human preferences or decisions under uncertainty. Traditional behavioral economics has widely studied rational choice ( Dreier, 1996 ) , and the corresponding algorithmic modeling to infer preferences relied on the transitivity and completeness assumptions. The formulation of transitivity includes two aspects: strict and weak. Strict transitivity states that one choice option is strictly preferred over another, while weak transitivity allows indifference between given choice options. Transitivity as a modeling assumption assumes that people can give consistent ranks to given choice options. However, this assumption may be violated mainly in a sequential judgment context ( Debreu, 1960 ; Bettman et al., 1998 ) since a previous preference may be inverted later in the process and result in a rock-paper-scissors relation due to context changes and cognitive biases ( Tversky and Kahneman, 1974 ) . Moreover, completeness assumes that people always have a preference, but this does not hold for decision-making under uncertain information, where in some cases, the preference may be undecided ( Ok et al., 2012 ) . Identifying the violation of the completeness assumption is more fundamental and complex by definition, as it is harder to define from a behavior perspective. Consequently, violating these assumptions can be framed as preference or decision uncertainty, and it is often strongly assumed that an inverted choice constitutes a noisy observation (e.g., ( González et al., 2017 ; Lin et al., 2022 ; Pfannschmidt et al., 2022 ; Benavoli et al., 2021 ) ) without a detailed inspection from the human perspective. 2.2. Modeling Human Feedback with Bayesian Optimization Bayesian optimization ( Močkus, 1975 ) is a technique used for the global optimization of expensive-to-evaluate functions. It builds a probabilistic model of the objective function and iteratively selects the next point to evaluate based on an acquisition function that balances exploration and exploitation. The model is updated as new evaluations are made, improving its accuracy over time. Bayesian optimization is beneficial when the objective function is black-box, expensive to evaluate, and multiple local optima exist. It has been successfully applied to various optimization problems in machine learning, engineering, and science ( Shahriari et al., 2016 ) . In addition to engineering aspects, BO can also model human feedback and enables HITL optimization ( Shahriari et al., 2016 ) utilizing, for example, biological measurements ( Kim et al., 2017 ; Ding et al., 2018 ) , interaction behavior ( Chong et al., 2021 ) , and measured preferential choices ( Brochu et al., 2007a ; González et al., 2017 ; Koyama et al., 2017 ) . It learns a posterior from the measured human feedback and aims to search for a global maximum of an unknown function by exploration and exploitation. In conjunction with measured human feedback, two popular genres of BO are actively being researched, as shown in Table 1 . Utility-based BO ( Močkus, 1975 ) requires measuring human feedback as a utility value. In contrast, preference-based BO (PBO) can propose examples using an acquisition function, ask the human to provide a choice, and infer the underlying preference iteratively. Table 1 . Examples of different Bayesian Optimization (BO) frameworks. Types of feedback can be either utility-based or preference-based. Most of the BO frameworks do not model indifference, and none of them consider incomplete preferences. Note that 1) rating can be considered either as absolute utility or preferential ranking distance depending on the underlying preference model, 2) selection is a special case of ranking where one item is strictly preferred over other options, and the ranking order of those unselected options is not specified, which means that their preference relation may be considered incomplete. Optimizer Input Form Feedback Type Options Modeled Indifference/Incompleteness Naive BO ( Močkus, 1975 ) Rating Utility Pointwise No/No 2GC ( Brochu et al., 2007a ) Selection Preferential Pairwise No/No PBO ( González et al., 2017 ) Selection Preferential Pairwise No/No EUBO ( Lin et al., 2022 ) Selection Preferential Pairwise No/No 4GC ( Brochu et al., 2010 ) Rating Preferential Listwise No/No SLS ( Koyama et al., 2017 ) Selection Preferential Listwise No/No SPS ( Koyama et al., 2020 ) Selection Preferential Listwise No/No PPBO ( Mikkola et al., 2020 ) Selection Preferential Listwise No/No Top-k BO ( Nguyen et al., 2021 ) Ranking Preferential Listwise Yes/No When dealing with preference-based human feedback, PBO as a specialized category of BO has received increasing development in recent studies ( González et al., 2017 ; Mikkola et al., 2020 ) . While BO learns based on absolute utility (e.g., absolute ratings of a given option), PBO learns relative rating or preferential selection as ranking information. To avoid the violations of the transitivity described above, the recent extensions ( Koyama et al., 2020 ; Siivola et al., 2021 ; Benavoli et al., 2021 ) of PBO transited from using a binary pairwise comparison to using a reasonable amount of options, resulting in a listwise comparison. These extensions could largely prevent violations of transitivity and infer more information at a time because they either consider choosing a set of options as winners among all given options ( Koyama et al., 2020 ; Benavoli et al., 2021 ) ; or provide a ranking of all given options, where options may share the same level of rank ( Siivola et al., 2021 ) . Note that more ranking elements may also increase the uncertainty for users and cause them to make imperfect decisions ( Monarch, 2021 ) due to increased workload. Thus, one should carefully consider the presented number of elements. Although PBO has used pairwise comparisons to mitigate various issues regarding unstable human judgment, these current approaches could also violate preference assumptions due to cognitive limitations. Tversky and Kahneman (1974) have widely presented how heuristic biases might influence the choice behavior. External causes can also produce a considerable amount of noisy observations in choice ( Kahneman et al., 2021 ) . To overcome the violation of preference assumptions, PBO has also considered handling noisy inputs ( Letham et al., 2019 ) and guarantees theoretical convergence when dealing with unstable choices. Despite all these developments in PBO, we still observe two challenges in practice. The first is that a human might change their objective during the optimization process, even when using pairwise comparisons. However, PBO assumes a fixed implicit underlying choice function that it can learn. Although PBO can handle noisy input, the other challenge is that it requires much more iterations to let the optimization converge. This is usually very costly when involving a human. We, therefore, need to design the UI carefully to mitigate these challenges and reduce errors. 2.3. Opinion Measurement Interfaces Figure 2 . Real-world measured opinions in different interfaces: a) Commonly used rating scales to measure opinion regarding one item; b) Two alternative candidates (non-)forced choice; c) Music album song orders without specified criteria, and forced ranking of conferences and movies using a distance. Conventional opinion measurement interfaces have different absolute measures, such as categorical choice and ordinal Likert-scale measures. The underlying analysis is based on Thurstone’s law of comparison ( Thurstone, 1927 ) . The optimal design of a pointwise measuring UI has been explored in psychology to reduce measuring error, for example, by asking repeated questions and checking the overall consistency ( Sherer et al., 1998 ) , regarding the influence of ticks ( Matejka et al., 2016 ) , or by allowing users to express uncertainty about their own input ( Greis et al., 2017 ) . Previous work also discussed improving rating accuracy in the HITL context ( Nguyen et al., 2013 ; Dudley and Kristensson, 2018 ) . A first systematic evaluation regarding the design space was provided by Nobarany et al. (2012) . They also observed that the rating interface might not be ideal for measuring opinions and discussed how to support ranking in the interface. In a way, this is similar to how PBO was designed ( Brochu et al., 2007a ; Brochu et al., 2010 ; González et al., 2017 ) ; opinion measurement interfaces that support comparison were also found beneficial here. Kalloori et al. (2018) discussed a few reasons for better-measured opinions using preference-based feedback: 1) Explicit rating utility suffers from calibration of drift, for concepts with different types of interpretations might lead to differently rated results. 2) Users might change their opinion from time to time due to anchoring ( Payne et al., 1993 ) . 3) Relative questions might potentially be faster and easier to answer. Due to the increased complexity of feedback types, ranking UIs are rarely explored, although there is initial work in this direction ( Luk, 1994 ; Neubarth, 2010 ) . Interfaces used in the Real World Opinions are frequently measured in real life for a variety of purposes. We can generally observe three genres of these UIs: pointwise, pairwise, and listwise UIs, as shown in Figure 2 . Interfaces used in HITL Optimization As shown in Figure 3 , many designs for opinion measurement interfaces are used in HITL optimization. Specifically, the presented examples can be treated as a mix of pairwise and listwise comparisons. The underlying feedback type that models the UI’s input form is either utility- or preference-based. Because of this diversity, we will provide a taxonomy to categorize them and determine our study design in the next section. Figure 3 . Examples of opinion measurement interfaces being used in HITL optimizations: a) A user chooses from a list of candidates to optimize illumination ( Marks et al., 1997 ) ; b) A user is asked to choose items that are closer to a given reference ( Wilber et al., 2014 ) ; c) A user is required to decide which of the two given options is closer to their desired material ( Brochu et al., 2007a ) ; d) A user is asked to choose which of two presented texts is more likely to be written on Wikipedia by a human ( Welleck et al., 2020 ) ; e) A user is required to choose which trained machine’s back-flip is better ( Christiano et al., 2017 ) , note that the interface uses a “can’t tell”; f) A user rates four presented graphics animations using a 3-step rating scale to show how close an animation is to what they are looking for ( Brochu et al., 2010 ) ; g) A user rates which of the given paired designs is more preferred ( Koyama et al., 2014 ) ; h) A user must select one target out of a list of choice alternatives ( Koyama et al., 2020 ) . i) A user ranks the given design variations, and each rank position has an associated ordinal rating label ( Ou et al., 2023 ) , and ties are allowed. These interfaces fit in a design space and are discussed in Section 3.1 . 3. Design Space We revisit the design space of opinion measurement interfaces and extend it to include multiple design variations of the listwise approach. Table 2 provides an overview of the design space of opinion measurement interfaces. The design space formally contains these two dimensions: the number of alternative options and the underlying feedback type . The number of alternative options encodes the complexity when measuring opinion. With more alternative options, we can gather more feedback from a user simultaneously. An interface is pointwise if it only measures the opinion regarding one item. Similarly, interfaces that measure information about two paired items are pairwise . With more than two options, the interface is listwise . For example, in Figure 2 a all interfaces are pointwise as they measure opinions regarding a single instance. Conceptually, a listwise interface also covers interfaces that potentially allow exploring infinite options (n= ∞ \infty , e.g., Koyama et al. (2017) ). However, regardless of the number of options, since a user has to select or mark a subset of preferential relations among all options, e.g., Wilber et al. (2014) , a multiple-item selection can be considered a strict preference between selected and unselected ones. In contrast, the preference order among (un)selected ones remains unspecified. Note that although an interface presents paired options to measure human opinion, it could still ask humans to estimate the distance between two options, which only conveys absolute distance utility as a rating regarding one item to the reference. Furthermore, although Figure 3 f presents four alternatives and asks how close they are to what the user is looking for, this is an absolute rating only concerning the user’s idea of an optimum (which remains unknown to everybody else). These considerations imply that the underlying feedback type, which the framed UI presents as a usage instruction, is also crucial for opinion measurement. The underlying type of feedback can be either utility -based or preference -based. Utility-based interfaces query a human to provide an absolute ordinal or cardinal value regarding an option (the interpretation of the value can differ depending on the context). Preference-based interfaces only measure relative information regarding paired options and, therefore, need further consideration to infer a latent utility. On the one hand, since utility-based interfaces only provide numeric information directly associated with the option, the relative information between options may not be explicit. However, we can sort the utility value. On the other hand, preference-based interfaces only provide local information. A hybrid feedback type provides a subtle design consideration to mix utility- and preference-based information. Similarly, we have two design alternatives, either strict or weak, depending on the type of preference. 3.1. Applicability We can place the previously presented examples into this design space. Figure 2 a contains 1-RS and n-RS: Twitter and Tinder only utilize binary responses regarding one option (like or not). The Amazon “by feature” rating example is n-RS but evaluates multiple dimensions using scales. In Figure 2 b, there are two examples of 2-AFC or 2-ANFC. Figure 2 c shows three listwise interfaces: n-AFR (songs are ranked without allowing ties and without information about how they are being ranked), n-AFRD (options ranked with a distance, items with the same utility value are forced to be placed on different ranks). In fact, Figure 3 a and Figure 3 h also use a meaningful 2D layout to present the alternative choices instead of a plain list. While this may improve the efficiency and user experience in specific tasks, it does not change the general structure and, therefore, the classification of the interface. Hypotheses Using this design space, we identified six promising opinion measurement interfaces, i.e., 1-RS, 2-ANFC, n n -RS, n n -AFR, n n -ANFR, n n -ANFRD (UI1 to UI6), see Figure 1 . Our selection is informed by results from related work, which hints that some might be better than others. Thus, we formulate four major hypotheses concerning the performance of HITL optimization when using such an interface: Hypothesis 1: Baseline Early work on HITL optimizations has shown great performance when using 2-ANFC ( Brochu et al., 2007a ; Brochu et al., 2007b ; Brochu et al., 2010 ) . Their results showed that 2-ANFC systems generally perform better than 1-RS and greatly support HITL systems. We use their initial findings as our baseline comparison and to validate our apparatus. Thus, we hypothesize ( H1 ) that the preference-based interface will outperform the utility-based interface regarding performance measures (UI1 vs. UI2). Hypothesis 2: Impact of Listwise Approach If H1 is true, this indicates that giving the user more options for comparison will improve the overall system performance. In fact, this is what findings by Cao et al. (2007) suggest. Thus, we hypothesize that a listwise comparison ( n > 2 n>2 ), will outperform comparisons with fewer options. As Listwise is the most flexible in terms of feedback, we next investigate the different strategies that emerged from related work ( Koyama et al., 2017 ; Koyama et al., 2020 ; Mikkola et al., 2020 ) . In this work, we investigate design variations in which the human can either give preferential ratings (e.g., Koyama et al. (2014) ), provide a strict ranking selection (e.g., Koyama et al. (2020) ), a weak ranking selection (e.g., Marks et al. (1997) ), or a combination of those (hybrid). Consequently, we hypothesize ( H2a ) that a listwise interface will outperform a pointwise interface when using utility-based feedback (UI1 vs. UI3). And we hypothesize ( H2b ) that a listwise interface will outperform a pairwise interface when using preference-based feedback (UI2 vs. UI5). Hypothesis 3: Impact of Listwise Design Variations Based on the initial findings by Mikkola et al. (2020) , we additionally hypothesize H3a and H3b . In detail, we hypothesize H3a that a preference-based listwise ranking interface will outperform a utility-based listwise rating interface (cf. ( Brochu et al., 2007b ; Brochu et al., 2007a ; Brochu et al., 2010 ) ) while allowing for expressing indifference (UI3 vs. UI5). Further, regarding indifference, we hypothesize H3b that being able to express indifference in the interface ( weak preference ) will be better than a forced choice ( strict preference ) (UI4 vs. UI5). Hypothesis 4: Impact of Hybrid Approach Based on hypotheses H1 - H3 and assuming that their outcome in this work is in line with prior work, Ou et al. (2023) used a new hybrid feedback interface. For this, n-ANFRD (UI6), we pick what we consider to be the best to support the HITL optimization, thus, getting the most information from the user. Thus, we hypothesize that the hybrid listwise interface will outperform: H4a the pairwise interface (UI2), H4b the listwise rating interface (UI3), H4c the listwise strict ranking interface (UI4), and H4d the listwise weak ranking interface (UI5). 5. User Study We conducted a user study to investigate how different opinion measurement interfaces impact the overall HITL optimization performance to answer our research questions ( RQ1 and RQ2 in Section 1 ) and verify our four hypotheses. Here, we compare the six user interfaces (6 conditions: UI1-UI6, Table 2 and Figure 1 ) using a between-subject design ( Interface ). We used tasks from two domains as a between-subject variable ( Domain ) to shorten the participation time and prevent a learning effect. One group did text summarization tasks from the natural language processing domain. The other group did image color enhancement tasks from the design domain. As dependent variables, we calculated interaction measures from usage logs and feedback from questionnaires (individual rating scales and open questions.) 5.1. User Interfaces As shown in Figure 1 , we selected six generic interfaces from this design space (1-RS, 2-ANFC, n n -RS, n n -AFR, n n -ANFR, n n -ANFRD) to facilitate our study design better. All interfaces are shown in Figure 4 for both tasks. The following describes the behavior of the six user interfaces: UI1 1-RS uses a bipolar slider-based Likert scale, similar to n n -RS. UI2 2-ANFC uses two radio buttons for preference indication. UI3 n-RS uses a bipolar slider-based Likert scale to indicate the preference for each option. UI4/5 n n -AFR requires a full ranking of all options, and the interface does not allow expressing indifference in this case, whereas n n -ANFR (UI5) can, which characterizes strict and weak preferences. To guarantee a pure ranking behavior in the interface, n n -AFR (UI4), and n n -ANFR (UI5) automatically adjust the distance between options. For example, if a user dropped two boxes on the 1st and 4th choice container box. Then the 4th choice will automatically move up to the 2nd choice and inform users that their ranking is automatically aligned and normalized. UI6 n n -ANFRD is the most flexible listwise ranking interface that permits users to place the option box in any given container box. Additionally, all interfaces include either checkbox options or container boxes to allow users to express incomplete preferences. 5.2. Task As many applications use HITL optimization, any domain with a set of system parameters to be determined could be used as a HITL optimization task. Examples of such domains are text summarization ( Simpson et al., 2020 ; Ou et al., 2023 ) , image color enhancement ( Koyama et al., 2016 ; Koyama et al., 2017 ; Koyama et al., 2020 ; Ou et al., 2023 ) , melody composition ( Zhou et al., 2021 ) , 3D meshing ( Ou et al., 2022 ; Ou et al., 2023 ) , 3D material design ( Brochu et al., 2007a ) , 3D animation ( Brochu et al., 2010 ) , and 3D illumination ( Marks et al., 1997 ) . In line with previous work ( Ou et al., 2023 ) , we selected text summarization and image color enhancement for the following reasons: First, text and image responses between client and server are easy to handle, lightweight, and fast. Second, the quality of text summarization and image color enhancement is a partly aesthetic judgment, for example, regarding the exact wording and color style. Therefore, it is still challenging to measure this quality objectively ( Bhandari et al., 2020 ; Ou et al., 2023 ) , making it plausible to bring a human into the loop. Optimizer Service and Bayesian Optimizers We used Bayesian optimization to give users new options based on their input history. As there is no one Bayesian optimizer to cater to the needs of all six interfaces, we selected the best Bayesian optimizer for each interface. In detail, UI1 and UI3 used naive BO ( Mockus et al., 1978 ) , UI2 used EUBO ( Lin et al., 2022 ) , and UI4-UI6 used the same advanced EUBO. While this could lead to performance differences, we perform benchmark comparisons to ensure they have equal performance; see Appendix A for full details. We used BoTorch ( Balandat et al., 2020 ) to implement all selected optimizers, which reads the user responses to estimate the next optimal system parameters for exploration. The Bayesian optimizer for rating-based interfaces (UI1 and UI3) used the Gaussian process as a surrogate model with Martern 5/2 kernel. The acquisition function is an expected improvement acquisition function that models noisy inputs ( Letham et al., 2019 ) . We used EUBO ( Lin et al., 2022 ) , a BO variate cf. Section 2.2 , as a state-of-the-art PBO optimizer that considers noisy inputs to estimate system parameters for the pairwise interface (UI2). The acquisition function is the Analytic Expected Utility Of Best Option acquisition function ( Lin et al., 2022 ) . The design of the EUBO algorithm guarantees that the current optimum is included in pairwise or listwise comparisons, and we can use the maximum posterior expected utility ( Chu and Ghahramani, 2005 ) to understand the impact on outcome utility. To guarantee fair comparisons and control experiment variables, instead of using different optimizers for all other listwise interfaces (i.e., UI4, UI5, and UI6), we extended EUBO to fit all listwise interfaces 5 5 5 See Supplemental Material for the implementation and further discussions on https://github.com/pytorch/botorch/discussions/1367 , last accessed: October 10, 2026 : We first fit a Gaussian process using the user’s rank data, then use the optimizer learned latent utility f ⁡ ( ⋅ ) f(\cdot) to fit another Gaussian process and infer the next batch of exploration positions. As EUBO maximizes the outcome utility difference between iterations, one can use the utility to analyze the optimization process. Moreover, in UI2 and UI4-UI6, although EUBO does not assume noiseless observations, we discarded indifference and incomplete preference input instead of generating a random preference order as 1) EUBO does not model indifference, 2) providing noisy input can decrease optimization performance and make a strong assumption about the preference model. These three Bayesian optimizers can optimize for our objectives and outperform pure random exploration in various simulated tasks, see Appendix A for comparisons. Figure 5 . The study procedure. Procedure The overall procedure for the participants is visualized in Figure 5 . Participants started the study with an informed consent form and answered initial demographic questions, including their age, gender, and levels of language proficiency. The opinion measurement interface then presents a set of evaluation options to the participants. The main task is to provide feedback, using the UI, to the AI to summarize the given news articles as much as possible while preserving the meaning of the article or enhance the image color as much as possible according to the preferences of the participants . Because the optimizers need initialization samples, in the first 4 iterations, a participant evaluated outcomes produced by quasi-random Sobol sampled ( Rezende et al., 2014 ; Wilson et al., 2017 ) system parameters. After acquiring these preference priors from participants, starting from the 5th iteration, the optimizer is used, and participants can freely terminate when satisfied with the current system outcomes. The task ends automatically after 20 iterations to limit participation time. After termination, participants answered six questions about their satisfaction with the system outcomes and their experience using the interface to provide feedback.
